items.stem: Which term is defined as "the production of ATP using energy released as electrons pass along the electron transport chain, coupled by chemiosmosis"?
items.answer: Oxidative phosphorylation
items.markingKey: Oxidative phosphorylation: the production of ATP using energy released as electrons pass along the electron transport chain, coupled by chemiosmosis.

items.stem: Explain why ATP is described as the universal energy currency.
items.answer: ATP is used in all organisms; it is made in respiration (or photosynthesis) and moved to where energy is needed; its hydrolysis releases energy in small, usable amounts for many different reactions.
items.markingKey: used in all cells/organisms [1]; made in one place and used in another / links energy-releasing and energy-requiring reactions [1]; small amounts released in one step [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why living organisms need a continuous supply of energy.
items.answer: Energy is needed for anabolic reactions, active transport, movement and (in mammals and birds) maintaining body temperature; energy is lost as heat at each transfer so it must be replaced.
items.markingKey: two named uses [2]; energy lost as heat / not recycled [1] [3]

items.stem: Grace reads that the complete oxidation of one mole of glucose releases 2870 kJ of energy and yields about 34 mol of ATP. Hydrolysis of ATP releases 30.5 kJ mol⁻¹. State what happens to the rest of the energy.
items.answer: It is released as heat (thermal energy).
items.markingKey: heat [1]; used to maintain body temperature in endotherms [1] [2]

items.stem: Omar reads that the complete oxidation of one mole of a fatty acid (palmitic acid) releases 9790 kJ of energy and yields about 108 mol of ATP. Hydrolysis of ATP releases 30.5 kJ mol⁻¹. (a) Calculate the percentage efficiency with which energy from the substrate is transferred to ATP. (b) A person respires 4.0 mol of a fatty acid (palmitic acid) in a day. Calculate the number of moles of ATP produced.

Scientists studying a sprinter found that mitochondria occupy about 26% of the volume of its fast-twitch muscle fibres, compared with about 5% in skin cells. (a) Give two reasons why ATP is suitable as the immediate energy source for these cells. (b) Explain why these cells release a lot of heat when active.
items.answer: (a) Hydrolysed in a single step (fast release); releases a small, manageable quantity of energy; soluble and moves easily; can be regenerated quickly. (b) Energy transfer in respiration and ATP hydrolysis is inefficient; much of the energy is released as heat.
items.markingKey: (a) any 2 from: Hydrolysed in a single step (fast release); releases a small, manageable quantity of energy; soluble and moves easily; can be regenerated quickly (1 mark each) [2] (b) inefficiency [1]; heat released in respiration / ATP use [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why ATP cannot be stored in large amounts and must be constantly regenerated.
items.answer: ATP is unstable (easily hydrolysed) and a cell contains only a small amount; it is used within seconds, so ADP and Pi are rephosphorylated continuously by respiration.
items.markingKey: unstable / easily hydrolysed [1]; only small quantity present / turnover [1]; ADP recycled by respiration [1] [3]

items.stem: An adult of mass 75 kg in Colombo hydrolyses about 40 kg of ATP per day, yet the body contains only about 250 g of ATP at any one time. The relative molecular mass of ATP is 507. (a) Calculate how many times, on average, each ATP molecule is recycled per day. (b) Using 30.5 kJ mol⁻¹, calculate the energy released per day by ATP hydrolysis.
items.answer: (a) 160 times (b) 2.4 MJ

items.stem: Mohammed reads that the complete oxidation of one mole of glucose releases 2880 kJ of energy and yields about 36 mol of ATP. Hydrolysis of ATP releases 31 kJ mol⁻¹. (a) Calculate the percentage efficiency with which energy from the substrate is transferred to ATP. (b) State what happens to the rest of the energy. (c) A person respires 2.5 mol of glucose in a day. Calculate the number of moles of ATP produced.
items.answer: (a) 38.8% (b) It is released as heat (thermal energy). (c) 90 mol
items.markingKey: (a) energy in ATP = 36 × 31 = 1116 kJ [1]; ÷ 2880 × 100 = 38.8% [1] [2] (b) heat [1]; used to maintain body temperature in endotherms [1] [2] (c) 2.5 × 36 = 90 mol [1]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "Krebs cycle"?
options: The removal of hydrogen from a molecule, catalysed by a dehydrogenase, usually with transfer to a coenzyme such as NAD.
The removal of carbon dioxide from a molecule.
A cycle of reactions in the mitochondrial matrix in which acetyl groups are oxidised, releasing CO₂ and forming reduced NAD, reduced FAD and ATP.
A coenzyme that carries acetyl groups from the link reaction into the Krebs cycle.
items.answer: A cycle of reactions in the mitochondrial matrix in which acetyl groups are oxidised, releasing CO₂ and forming reduced NAD, reduced FAD and ATP.
items.markingKey: Krebs cycle: a cycle of reactions in the mitochondrial matrix in which acetyl groups are oxidised, releasing CO₂ and forming reduced NAD, reduced FAD and ATP.

items.stem: Explain why the Krebs cycle is described as a cycle.
items.answer: Oxaloacetate (4C) accepts the acetyl group to form citrate and is regenerated at the end of the sequence, so it can accept another acetyl group.
items.markingKey: oxaloacetate combines with acetyl CoA [1]; oxaloacetate regenerated [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the Krebs cycle cannot continue in the absence of oxygen even though no oxygen is used in the cycle itself.
items.answer: Without oxygen as the final electron acceptor the ETC stops, so reduced NAD and FAD are not reoxidised; no NAD/FAD is available to accept hydrogen in the dehydrogenation steps, so the cycle stops.
items.markingKey: oxygen is final electron acceptor [1]; reduced NAD/FAD not reoxidised [1]; no NAD/FAD for dehydrogenation [1] [3]

items.stem: How many molecules of reduced NAD are produced in glycolysis and the link reaction from one molecule of glucose?
items.markingKey: glycolysis: 2 per glucose; the link reaction: 2 per glucose = 4.

items.stem: How many molecules of ATP (net gain) are produced in glycolysis from 5 molecules of glucose?
items.markingKey: glycolysis: 2 per glucose; × 5 = 10.

items.stem: Calculate how many molecules of ATP (net gain) are produced in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle from one molecule of glucose. Show your working, treating each stage separately.
items.markingKey: glycolysis: 2 per glucose; the Krebs cycle: 2 per glucose = 4. Per-stage values [1]; correct total [1] [2]

items.stem: Daniel isolated mitochondria from potato tuber and suspended them in a buffered solution containing pyruvate, ADP, Pi and oxygen. Over 20 minutes, 5 μmol of pyruvate were completely oxidised. (a) Explain why glucose was not used as the substrate. (b) Explain why ADP and Pi were included in the solution.
items.answer: (a) Mitochondria cannot use glucose: glycolysis enzymes are in the cytoplasm and there is no glucose carrier in the outer/inner membrane; pyruvate is the substrate that enters mitochondria. (b) They are needed for ATP synthesis (substrate-linked and oxidative phosphorylation); without them chemiosmosis stops and so electron transport and the Krebs cycle slow down.
items.markingKey: (a) glycolysis in cytoplasm [1]; glucose cannot enter / pyruvate enters mitochondria [1] [2] (b) needed for ATP synthesis [1]; respiration coupled to ATP synthesis [1] [2]

items.stem: Ana isolated mitochondria from beef heart and suspended them in a buffered solution containing pyruvate, ADP, Pi and oxygen. Over 20 minutes, 5 μmol of pyruvate were completely oxidised. (a) Calculate how many μmol of carbon dioxide were released. (b) Explain why glucose was not used as the substrate. (c) Name the location within the mitochondrion where the link reaction and Krebs cycle take place.
items.answer: (a) 15 μmol (b) Mitochondria cannot use glucose: glycolysis enzymes are in the cytoplasm and there is no glucose carrier in the outer/inner membrane; pyruvate is the substrate that enters mitochondria. (c) The matrix.
items.markingKey: (a) each pyruvate: 1 CO₂ in link reaction + 2 in Krebs cycle = 3 [1]; 5 × 3 = 15 μmol [1] [2] (b) glycolysis in cytoplasm [1]; glucose cannot enter / pyruvate enters mitochondria [1] [2] (c) The matrix [1]

items.stem: Where in a eukaryotic cell does glycolysis take place?
items.answer: Cytoplasm
items.markingKey: Glycolysis is in the cytoplasm; link and Krebs in the matrix.

items.stem: Describe what happens to pyruvate in the link reaction.
items.answer: Pyruvate is actively transported into the matrix; it is decarboxylated (CO₂ removed) and dehydrogenated (NAD reduced); the 2C acetyl group combines with coenzyme A to form acetyl CoA.
items.markingKey: enters matrix [1]; decarboxylation [1]; dehydrogenation / reduced NAD [1]; acetyl CoA formed [1] [4]

items.stem: Explain how glycolysis produces a net gain of ATP.
items.answer: Two ATP are used to phosphorylate the hexose; each of the two triose phosphates is oxidised and converted to pyruvate, producing 2 ATP by substrate-linked phosphorylation, so 4 are made in total: net gain of 2.
items.markingKey: 2 ATP used [1]; 4 ATP made by substrate-linked phosphorylation [1]; net 2 [1] [3]

items.stem: Grace supplies root tip cells with a substrate containing carbon-14 in the acetyl group of acetyl CoA. Predict where the label will appear and explain your answer.
items.answer: In citrate, then the 5C and 4C compounds and eventually CO₂ in later turns of the cycle: acetyl group joins oxaloacetate to form citrate; carbons are released as CO₂ in later turns.
items.markingKey: correct molecule [1]; reason (acetyl group joins oxaloacetate to form citrate; carbons are released as CO₂ in later turns) [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe the stages of glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle.
items.answer: Glycolysis (cytoplasm): glucose phosphorylated twice using 2 ATP to fructose bisphosphate; split into 2 triose phosphate; oxidised (NAD reduced) to pyruvate; 4 ATP by substrate-linked phosphorylation (net 2). Link (matrix): pyruvate decarboxylated and dehydrogenated, acetyl CoA. Krebs: acetyl + oxaloacetate → citrate (6C); decarboxylations to 5C and 4C; reduced NAD ×3, FAD ×1, ATP ×1 per turn; oxaloacetate regenerated.
items.markingKey: glycolysis phosphorylation and splitting [2]; oxidation and ATP yield [1]; link reaction [2]; Krebs citrate [1]; decarboxylation / dehydrogenation / products per turn [2] [8]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "intermembrane space"?
options: The synthesis of ATP driven by the diffusion of protons down their electrochemical gradient through ATP synthase.
A substance that makes the inner membrane leaky to protons so that electron transport continues but ATP synthesis stops.
A series of electron carrier proteins in the inner mitochondrial membrane that pass electrons from reduced NAD/FAD to oxygen, releasing energy used to pump protons.
The narrow region between the outer and inner mitochondrial membranes into which protons are pumped.
items.answer: The narrow region between the outer and inner mitochondrial membranes into which protons are pumped.
items.markingKey: Intermembrane space: the narrow region between the outer and inner mitochondrial membranes into which protons are pumped.

items.stem: Explain how the electron transport chain produces a proton gradient.
items.answer: Reduced NAD/FAD donate electrons (and protons) to the chain; electrons pass along carriers by redox reactions, releasing energy; this energy is used by carrier proteins to pump protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space.
items.markingKey: electrons from reduced NAD/FAD [1]; redox / energy released as electrons pass [1]; protons pumped into intermembrane space [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain how ATP is synthesised by chemiosmosis in a mitochondrion.
items.answer: High proton concentration in the intermembrane space; inner membrane impermeable to protons; protons diffuse back into the matrix through ATP synthase down their electrochemical gradient; this causes the enzyme to rotate/change shape and catalyse ADP + Pi → ATP.
items.markingKey: proton gradient [1]; membrane impermeable except via ATP synthase [1]; diffusion through ATP synthase [1]; ADP + Pi → ATP [1] [4]

items.stem: Assume that each reduced NAD gives 2.5 ATP and each reduced FAD gives 1.5 ATP by oxidative phosphorylation. What is the total number of ATP molecules made from one glucose molecule as a result of the Krebs cycle, including any ATP made by substrate-linked phosphorylation.
items.markingKey: reduced NAD = 6, reduced FAD = 2 [1]; 6 × 2.5 + 2 × 1.5 = 18 [1]; + 2 substrate-linked = 20 [1] [3]

items.stem: Assume that each reduced NAD gives 2.5 ATP and each reduced FAD gives 1.5 ATP by oxidative phosphorylation. Calculate the total number of ATP molecules made from one glucose molecule as a result of the Krebs cycle, including any ATP made by substrate-linked phosphorylation.
items.answer: 20 ATP
items.markingKey: reduced NAD = 6, reduced FAD = 2 [1]; 6 × 2.5 + 2 × 1.5 = 18 [1]; + 2 substrate-linked = 20 [1] [3]

items.stem: Assume that each reduced NAD gives 2.5 ATP and each reduced FAD gives 1.5 ATP by oxidative phosphorylation. Calculate the total number of ATP molecules made from one glucose molecule as a result of the Krebs cycle, including any ATP made by substrate-linked phosphorylation. Suggest why the number of ATP molecules actually made is usually lower.
items.answer: 20 ATP; actual yield lower because of proton leakage and energy used to transport pyruvate/ADP/Pi into the mitochondrion.
items.markingKey: reduced NAD = 6, reduced FAD = 2 [1]; 6 × 2.5 + 2 × 1.5 = 18 [1]; + 2 substrate-linked = 20 [1] proton leak or transport cost [1] [4]

items.stem: Mohammed investigates two respiratory poisons on a suspension of isolated mitochondria supplied with a substrate, ADP and Pi. Oligomycin blocks the proton channel of ATP synthase. DNP acts as an uncoupler, carrying protons across the inner membrane. (a) Predict the effects of DNP on oxygen uptake and ATP synthesis. (b) Explain why oxygen uptake can be used as a measure of the rate of electron transport.
items.answer: (a) Oxygen uptake continues (or rises); ATP synthesis falls; heat production rises. (b) Oxygen is the final electron acceptor; each pair of electrons that passes along the chain reduces half an oxygen molecule to water, so oxygen use is proportional to electron flow.
items.markingKey: (a) oxygen uptake continues (or rises); ATP synthesis falls; heat production rises [2] (b) oxygen final acceptor [1]; proportional to electron flow [1] [2]

items.stem: Felix investigates two respiratory poisons on a suspension of isolated mitochondria supplied with a substrate, ADP and Pi. Oligomycin blocks the proton channel of ATP synthase. Cyanide inhibits cytochrome oxidase, the last carrier, so electrons cannot pass to oxygen. (a) Explain why oxygen uptake can be used as a measure of the rate of electron transport. (b) Explain why electron transport and ATP synthesis are described as coupled.
items.answer: (a) Oxygen is the final electron acceptor; each pair of electrons that passes along the chain reduces half an oxygen molecule to water, so oxygen use is proportional to electron flow. (b) Electron transport pumps protons; the proton gradient is used to make ATP; if ATP synthesis stops, the gradient builds up and slows electron transport.
items.markingKey: (a) oxygen final acceptor [1]; proportional to electron flow [1] [2] (b) gradient links the two [1]; one cannot normally occur without the other [1] [2]

items.stem: Where are the electron carriers of the electron transport chain located in a mitochondrion?
items.answer: Inner mitochondrial membrane
items.markingKey: On the cristae.

items.stem: Explain why cyanide, which inhibits the final carrier (cytochrome oxidase), quickly stops ATP synthesis.
items.answer: Electrons cannot pass to oxygen, so the chain backs up; no electron flow means no protons pumped; the proton gradient is lost and ATP synthase stops; NAD is not regenerated so the Krebs cycle also stops.
items.markingKey: electron flow stops [1]; no proton pumping / gradient [1]; no chemiosmosis / ATP [1]; NAD not regenerated [1] [4]

items.stem: Assume that each reduced NAD gives 2.5 ATP and each reduced FAD gives 1.5 ATP by oxidative phosphorylation. What is the total number of ATP molecules made from one glucose molecule as a result of the link reaction, including any ATP made by substrate-linked phosphorylation.
items.markingKey: reduced NAD = 2, reduced FAD = 0 [1]; 2 × 2.5 + 0 × 1.5 = 5 [1]; + 0 substrate-linked = 5 [1] [3]

items.stem: Diego measured the pH in the matrix of actively respiring mitochondria as 7.8 and in the intermembrane space as 6.8. Explain how this difference in pH is produced.
items.answer: Energy from electrons passing along the ETC is used to pump protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space.
items.markingKey: ETC / electron flow [1]; protons pumped into intermembrane space [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe how oxidative phosphorylation produces ATP in a mitochondrion.
items.answer: Reduced NAD and FAD release H; H splits into H⁺ and e⁻; electrons passed along carriers in inner membrane (redox); energy released pumps H⁺ into intermembrane space; proton gradient; H⁺ diffuse through ATP synthase; ADP + Pi → ATP; oxygen final electron acceptor forming water; NAD regenerated.
items.markingKey: H from reduced NAD/FAD [1]; electrons along carriers [1]; energy pumps protons [1]; gradient [1]; ATP synthase [1]; ADP + Pi [1]; oxygen + water [1] [7]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "lactate fermentation"?
options: Anaerobic respiration in mammalian muscle in which pyruvate is reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase, regenerating NAD.
The ratio of the volume of carbon dioxide given out to the volume of oxygen taken in during respiration in a given time (RQ = CO₂ ÷ O₂).
The extra oxygen taken in after exercise to oxidise lactate (in the liver) and restore ATP and creatine phosphate levels.
Tissue with large air spaces found in rice stems and roots that allows oxygen to diffuse to submerged tissues.
items.answer: Anaerobic respiration in mammalian muscle in which pyruvate is reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase, regenerating NAD.
items.markingKey: Lactate fermentation: anaerobic respiration in mammalian muscle in which pyruvate is reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase, regenerating NAD.

items.stem: Explain why far less ATP is produced in anaerobic respiration than in aerobic respiration.
items.answer: Only glycolysis produces ATP (net 2); without oxygen the ETC cannot accept electrons, so no oxidative phosphorylation; link reaction and Krebs cycle stop; much energy remains in lactate or ethanol.
items.markingKey: only glycolysis [1]; no ETC / oxidative phosphorylation [1]; Krebs stops [1]; energy left in product [1] [4]

items.stem: Explain why an RQ greater than 1 suggests that some anaerobic respiration is taking place.
items.answer: Anaerobic respiration in yeast/plants produces CO₂ without using oxygen, so CO₂ given out exceeds O₂ taken in.
items.markingKey: CO₂ produced without O₂ uptake [1]; ratio > 1 [1] [2]

items.stem: The equation for the complete aerobic respiration of tripalmitin is C₅₁H₉₈O₆ + 72.5O₂ → 51CO₂ + 49H₂O. Calculate the respiratory quotient (RQ).
Stearic acid has the formula C₁₈H₃₆O₂. Construct a balanced equation for its complete aerobic respiration and calculate the RQ.
items.answer: C₁₈H₃₆O₂ + 26O₂ → 18CO₂ + 18H₂O; RQ = 0.69

items.stem: Rice is grown in flooded paddy fields in Santiago. In waterlogged conditions the roots of most plants die, but rice roots survive. Researchers found that alcohol dehydrogenase activity in rice roots rose by 10 times after flooding. (a) Explain the advantage of the increase in alcohol dehydrogenase activity. (b) State the products of anaerobic respiration in rice root cells.
items.answer: (a) Ethanal is reduced to ethanol more rapidly, so NAD is regenerated and glycolysis can continue to provide ATP. (b) Ethanol, carbon dioxide and a small amount of ATP.
items.markingKey: (a) NAD regenerated [1]; glycolysis / ATP continues [1] [2] (b) Ethanol [1]; carbon dioxide and a small amount of ATP [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why lipids have a lower RQ than carbohydrates.
items.answer: Lipids contain relatively little oxygen and more hydrogen, so more oxygen is needed to oxidise the hydrogen to water for each CO₂ produced.
items.markingKey: less oxygen in molecule / more H [1]; more O₂ needed per CO₂ [1] [2]

items.stem: In 15 minutes, germinating pea seeds took in 2.31 cm³ of oxygen and gave out 1.87 cm³ of carbon dioxide. (a) Calculate the respiratory quotient. (b) Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake per hour.

Leila mixed 10 g of yeast with glucose solution in a sealed flask in Karachi. After the oxygen was used up, carbon dioxide was still released and ethanol accumulated. (a) Describe the reactions by which yeast converts pyruvate to ethanol. (b) Explain why the yeast population eventually stopped growing. (c) Calculate the theoretical maximum ratio of ATP produced per glucose by aerobic respiration to that produced by anaerobic respiration, using 32 ATP for aerobic respiration.
items.answer: (a) Pyruvate is decarboxylated to ethanal by pyruvate decarboxylase (CO₂ released); ethanal is reduced to ethanol by alcohol dehydrogenase using reduced NAD. (b) Ethanol accumulated to toxic concentrations / glucose was used up; little ATP is made by anaerobic respiration. (c) 16 : 1
items.markingKey: (a) decarboxylation to ethanal [1]; reduction to ethanol [1]; NAD regenerated [1] [3] (b) ethanol toxic [1]; substrate used up / little ATP [1] [2] (c) 32 ÷ 2 = 16 [1]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "compensating tube"?
options: A solid that absorbs carbon dioxide, used in a respirometer so that changes in volume are due to oxygen uptake only.
A redox indicator that is blue when oxidised and colourless when reduced by dehydrogenase activity in respiring cells.
Apparatus that measures the rate of oxygen uptake by respiring organisms from the movement of a fluid in a capillary tube.
A second tube containing no organisms, used to cancel out effects of changes in temperature and pressure.
items.answer: A second tube containing no organisms, used to cancel out effects of changes in temperature and pressure.
items.markingKey: Compensating tube: a second tube containing no organisms, used to cancel out effects of changes in temperature and pressure.

items.stem: What is the name for "a solid that absorbs carbon dioxide, used in a respirometer so that changes in volume are due to oxygen uptake only"?
items.answer: Soda lime
items.markingKey: Soda lime: a solid that absorbs carbon dioxide, used in a respirometer so that changes in volume are due to oxygen uptake only.

items.stem: Explain why a respirometer containing organisms is left in the water bath for several minutes before readings are taken.
items.answer: To allow the apparatus and organisms to reach the temperature of the water bath (equilibrate), so that changes in volume are due to respiration and not gas expansion or contraction.
items.markingKey: equilibrate to temperature [1]; avoids volume changes from heating/cooling [1] [2]

items.stem: Amara placed 2 g of germinating barley grains in a respirometer containing soda lime at 25 °C. The coloured fluid in the capillary tube (internal diameter 0.5 mm) moved 55 mm in 20 minutes. Explain why the fluid moved towards the organisms.
items.answer: Oxygen was taken up and the CO₂ released was absorbed by the soda lime, so the volume (pressure) of gas in the tube fell.
items.markingKey: O₂ used [1]; CO₂ absorbed so volume falls [1] [2]

items.stem: Chloe measured the rate of respiration of 5 g samples of germinating seeds at different temperatures using a respirometer containing soda lime. The distance moved by the fluid in the capillary tube in 10 minutes was recorded. Results table. Temperature / °C: 5, 15, 25, 35, 45. Distance moved by fluid in 10 minutes / mm, trial 1: 7, 14, 27, 54, 17; trial 2: 7, 14, 27, 51, 17; trial 3: 8, 15, 28, 53, 17. (a) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation. (b) Suggest one way to improve this investigation.
items.answer: (a) Independent: temperature; dependent: distance moved by fluid in 10 minutes. (b) Use a thermostatically controlled water bath.
items.markingKey: (a) independent variable = temperature [1]; dependent variable = distance moved by fluid in 10 minutes [1] [2] (b) Any one from: use a thermostatically controlled water bath; use a syringe to reset the fluid and a larger number of seeds; use a compensating tube with glass beads to allow for pressure changes; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the temperature (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1]

items.stem: Explain how a respirometer could be used to measure the RQ of germinating seeds.
items.answer: Measure volume change with KOH (O₂ uptake, x); repeat without KOH (difference between O₂ uptake and CO₂ output, y); CO₂ = x − y (if movement towards seeds is positive); RQ = (x − y) ÷ x.
items.markingKey: with KOH gives O₂ [1]; without KOH gives O₂ − CO₂ [1]; calculation of RQ [1] [3]

items.stem: Which molecules are produced when ATP is hydrolysed?
items.answer: ADP and inorganic phosphate
items.markingKey: ATP + H₂O → ADP + Pi, releasing about 30.5 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.stem: Explain the role of ATP in the active transport of sodium and potassium ions across a cell surface membrane.
items.answer: ATP is hydrolysed by the carrier protein (an ATPase); the phosphate binds to the protein and changes its shape, so 3 Na⁺ are moved out and 2 K⁺ in against their concentration gradients.
items.markingKey: ATP hydrolysed by carrier / ATPase [1]; phosphorylation causes shape change [1]; ions moved against gradient [1] [3]

items.stem: An adult of mass 60 kg in Dubai hydrolyses about 65 kg of ATP per day, yet the body contains only about 100 g of ATP at any one time. The relative molecular mass of ATP is 507. Calculate how many times, on average, each ATP molecule is recycled per day.
items.answer: 650 times

items.stem: Scientists studying a hummingbird found that mitochondria occupy about 29% of the volume of its flight muscle cells, compared with about 5% in skin cells. (a) Explain the difference in mitochondrial volume. (b) Give two reasons why ATP is suitable as the immediate energy source for these cells. (c) Explain why these cells release a lot of heat when active.
items.answer: (a) Flight muscle cells have a very high demand for ATP (e.g. for contraction / active processes); more mitochondria allow more aerobic respiration and oxidative phosphorylation. (b) Hydrolysed in a single step (fast release); releases a small, manageable quantity of energy; soluble and moves easily; can be regenerated quickly. (c) Energy transfer in respiration and ATP hydrolysis is inefficient; much of the energy is released as heat.
items.markingKey: (a) high ATP demand linked to function [1]; mitochondria site of most ATP synthesis / Krebs and ETC [1] [2] (b) any 2 from: Hydrolysed in a single step (fast release); releases a small, manageable quantity of energy; soluble and moves easily; can be regenerated quickly (1 mark each) [2] (c) inefficiency [1]; heat released in respiration / ATP use [1] [2]

items.stem: Which compound combines with acetyl coenzyme A at the start of the Krebs cycle?
items.answer: Oxaloacetate (4C)
items.markingKey: Acetyl (2C) + oxaloacetate (4C) → citrate (6C).

items.stem: Explain the importance of dehydrogenation reactions in the Krebs cycle.
items.answer: Hydrogen atoms removed are accepted by NAD and FAD; the reduced coenzymes carry hydrogen (electrons) to the ETC, where most of the ATP is made by oxidative phosphorylation.
items.markingKey: hydrogen to NAD/FAD [1]; carried to ETC [1]; most ATP made there [1] [3]

items.stem: How many molecules of reduced FAD are produced in glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle from one molecule of glucose?
items.markingKey: glycolysis: 0 per glucose; the link reaction: 0 per glucose; the Krebs cycle: 2 per glucose = 2.

items.stem: Lucas supplies cultured muscle cells with a substrate containing carbon-14 in the acetyl group of acetyl CoA. Predict where the label will appear and explain your answer.
items.answer: In citrate, then the 5C and 4C compounds and eventually CO₂ in later turns of the cycle: acetyl group joins oxaloacetate to form citrate; carbons are released as CO₂ in later turns.
items.markingKey: correct molecule [1]; reason (acetyl group joins oxaloacetate to form citrate; carbons are released as CO₂ in later turns) [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how the structure of a mitochondrion is adapted for its functions in respiration.
items.answer: Outer membrane with transport proteins (pyruvate entry); matrix contains Krebs and link reaction enzymes, coenzymes, mitochondrial DNA and 70S ribosomes; inner membrane folded into cristae giving large surface area for ETC and ATP synthase; inner membrane impermeable to protons; small intermembrane space allows proton gradient to build quickly.
items.markingKey: matrix enzymes / link and Krebs [2]; cristae surface area [1]; ETC and ATP synthase on inner membrane [1]; impermeable to H⁺ [1]; intermembrane space [1]; DNA/ribosomes to make own proteins [1] [7]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "final electron acceptor"?
options: Oxygen, which combines with electrons and protons at the end of the electron transport chain to form water.
The folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane that give a large surface area for electron carriers and ATP synthase.
A substance that makes the inner membrane leaky to protons so that electron transport continues but ATP synthesis stops.
The narrow region between the outer and inner mitochondrial membranes into which protons are pumped.
items.answer: Oxygen, which combines with electrons and protons at the end of the electron transport chain to form water.
items.markingKey: Final electron acceptor: oxygen, which combines with electrons and protons at the end of the electron transport chain to form water.

items.stem: Explain why the inner mitochondrial membrane being impermeable to protons is essential for ATP synthesis.
items.answer: Protons can only return through ATP synthase, so the gradient is maintained and its energy is used to make ATP; leakage would dissipate the gradient as heat.
items.markingKey: gradient maintained [1]; protons forced through ATP synthase [1] [2]

items.stem: Assume that each reduced NAD gives 3 ATP and each reduced FAD gives 2 ATP by oxidative phosphorylation. What is the total number of ATP molecules made from one glucose molecule as a result of glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle, including any ATP made by substrate-linked phosphorylation.
items.markingKey: reduced NAD = 10, reduced FAD = 2 [1]; 10 × 3 + 2 × 2 = 34 [1]; + 4 substrate-linked = 38 [1] [3]

items.stem: Mohammed measured the pH in the matrix of actively respiring mitochondria as 8 and in the intermembrane space as 7. (a) Predict the effect of adding an uncoupler such as DNP on the pH difference and explain your answer. (b) Explain how this pH difference is used to make ATP.
items.answer: (a) The difference would decrease (pH values become similar) because protons leak back across the membrane without passing through ATP synthase. (b) Protons diffuse down their gradient through ATP synthase into the matrix; this drives phosphorylation of ADP to ATP (chemiosmosis).
items.markingKey: (a) difference falls [1]; protons leak back / gradient dissipated [1] [2] (b) diffusion through ATP synthase [1]; ADP + Pi → ATP [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain the effects of cyanide on a cell, starting from its effect on the electron transport chain.
items.answer: Inhibits cytochrome oxidase; electrons not passed to oxygen; chain stops; no proton pumping; no ATP from chemiosmosis; reduced NAD/FAD not oxidised so NAD/FAD unavailable; Krebs and link reaction stop; only glycolysis with anaerobic regeneration of NAD; ATP-requiring processes (active transport, contraction) fail; lactate builds up; cell death.
items.markingKey: site of action [1]; electron flow stops [1]; no proton gradient / ATP [1]; NAD not regenerated [1]; Krebs stops [1]; anaerobic only, little ATP [1]; consequence for cell [1] [7]

items.stem: Germinating seeds give out 8.4 cm³ CO₂ while taking in 12.0 cm³ O₂. Which substrate are they most likely respiring?
items.answer: Lipid

items.stem: Compare anaerobic respiration in mammals and yeast.
items.answer: Both: glycolysis, 2 ATP, NAD regenerated by reducing pyruvate (product). Mammals: pyruvate → lactate, one step, no CO₂, reversible. Yeast: pyruvate → ethanal + CO₂ → ethanol, two steps, irreversible.
items.markingKey: similarity [1]; lactate vs ethanol [1]; CO₂ released only in yeast [1]; reversibility / number of steps [1] [4]

items.stem: In 20 minutes, maggots took in 0.82 cm³ of oxygen and gave out 0.67 cm³ of carbon dioxide. Calculate the respiratory quotient.
In a respirometer without KOH, the fluid does not move while germinating peas respire. What does this suggest?
options: The peas are respiring lipid only
The volume of CO₂ released equals the volume of O₂ absorbed
items.answer: The volume of CO₂ released equals the volume of O₂ absorbed
items.markingKey: RQ = 1, carbohydrate substrate.

items.stem: Amara measured the rate of respiration of 5 g samples of germinating seeds at different temperatures using a respirometer containing soda lime. The distance moved by the fluid in the capillary tube in 10 minutes was recorded. Results table. Temperature / °C: 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35. Distance moved by fluid in 10 minutes / mm, trial 1: 11, 16, 23, 29, 41, 59; trial 2: 11, 16, 21, 30, 42, 56; trial 3: 11, 22, 22, 30, 42, 57. State two variables that should be kept constant in this investigation.
items.answer: Mass of seeds; type and age of seeds.
items.markingKey: Any two from: mass of seeds; type and age of seeds; volume of soda lime; time allowed for equilibration; diameter of capillary tube; time interval [2]

items.stem: Yusuf measured the rate of respiration of 5 g samples of germinating seeds at different temperatures using a respirometer containing soda lime. The distance moved by the fluid in the capillary tube in 10 minutes was recorded. Results table. Temperature / °C: 5, 15, 25, 35, 45. Distance moved by fluid in 10 minutes / mm, trial 1: 8, 16, 30, 59, 29; trial 2: 8, 16, 31, 58, 20; trial 3: 8, 16, 31, 59, 19. (a) Explain the results. (b) The capillary tube has a radius of 0.5 mm. Calculate the volume of oxygen absorbed at the highest temperature tested.
items.answer: (a) As temperature rises, enzymes (e.g. dehydrogenases) and substrates have more kinetic energy, so there are more successful collisions and respiration is faster; at high temperatures enzymes denature and the rate falls. (b) 15.3 mm³
items.markingKey: (a) kinetic energy / collisions [1]; enzymes in respiration named [1]; denaturation at high temperature [1] [3] (b) π × 0.5² × 19.5 [1] = 15.3 mm³ [1] [2]

items.stem: Approximately how much energy is released by hydrolysis of one mole of ATP to ADP and Pi?
items.markingKey: The standard value used is about 30.5 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.stem: Explain why a cell with a high rate of protein synthesis contains many mitochondria.
items.answer: Peptide bond formation and tRNA charging require ATP; mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration (Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation) and produce most of the cell's ATP.
items.markingKey: protein synthesis needs ATP [1]; mitochondria site of aerobic respiration / most ATP [1] [2]

items.stem: Kenji reads that the complete oxidation of one mole of a fatty acid (palmitic acid) releases 9790 kJ of energy and yields about 108 mol of ATP. Hydrolysis of ATP releases 30.5 kJ mol⁻¹. Suggest why the actual yield of ATP per mole of substrate in a cell is often lower than the theoretical value.
items.answer: Some protons leak back across the inner membrane without passing through ATP synthase; energy is used to transport ADP/Pi and pyruvate into the mitochondrion; some reduced NAD from glycolysis enters via a shuttle giving less ATP.
items.markingKey: proton leakage [1]; energy used for transport into mitochondrion / shuttle [1] [2]

items.stem: Scientists studying an electric eel found that mitochondria occupy about 39% of the volume of its electrocyte cells, compared with about 5% in skin cells. (a) Give two reasons why ATP is suitable as the immediate energy source for these cells. (b) Suggest why these cells also contain a store of creatine phosphate. (c) Explain why these cells release a lot of heat when active.
items.answer: (a) Hydrolysed in a single step (fast release); releases a small, manageable quantity of energy; soluble and moves easily; can be regenerated quickly. (b) Creatine phosphate can rapidly donate a phosphate to ADP to regenerate ATP during short bursts of activity, faster than respiration can supply it. (c) Energy transfer in respiration and ATP hydrolysis is inefficient; much of the energy is released as heat.
items.markingKey: (a) any 2 from: Hydrolysed in a single step (fast release); releases a small, manageable quantity of energy; soluble and moves easily; can be regenerated quickly (1 mark each) [2] (b) regenerates ATP from ADP [1]; rapid / during sudden high demand [1] [2] (c) inefficiency [1]; heat released in respiration / ATP use [1] [2]

items.stem: How many carbon atoms are in a molecule of citrate?
items.markingKey: Citrate is a 6C compound.

items.stem: A student in Riyadh states: "The Krebs cycle produces most of the ATP made in aerobic respiration." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: The Krebs cycle makes only 2 ATP per glucose directly; its main role is producing reduced NAD and FAD for oxidative phosphorylation, which makes most ATP.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: The Krebs cycle makes only 2 ATP per glucose directly; its main role is producing reduced NAD and FAD for oxidative phosphorylation, which makes most ATP. [2]

items.stem: How many molecules of reduced FAD are produced in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle from one molecule of glucose?
items.markingKey: glycolysis: 0 per glucose; the Krebs cycle: 2 per glucose = 2.

items.stem: Omar supplies yeast cells with a substrate containing carbon-14 in the acetyl group of acetyl CoA. Predict where the label will appear and explain your answer.
items.answer: In citrate, then the 5C and 4C compounds and eventually CO₂ in later turns of the cycle: acetyl group joins oxaloacetate to form citrate; carbons are released as CO₂ in later turns.
items.markingKey: correct molecule [1]; reason (acetyl group joins oxaloacetate to form citrate; carbons are released as CO₂ in later turns) [1] [2]

items.stem: Elena isolated mitochondria from beef heart and suspended them in a buffered solution containing pyruvate, ADP, Pi and oxygen. Over 20 minutes, 6 μmol of pyruvate were completely oxidised. (a) Calculate how many μmol of carbon dioxide were released. (b) Predict and explain the effect of removing oxygen from the suspension. (c) Explain why ADP and Pi were included in the solution.
items.answer: (a) 18 μmol (b) CO₂ release would stop: no final electron acceptor, so reduced NAD/FAD are not oxidised; no NAD/FAD for the link reaction and Krebs cycle. (c) They are needed for ATP synthesis (substrate-linked and oxidative phosphorylation); without them chemiosmosis stops and so electron transport and the Krebs cycle slow down.
items.markingKey: (a) each pyruvate: 1 CO₂ in link reaction + 2 in Krebs cycle = 3 [1]; 6 × 3 = 18 μmol [1] [2] (b) CO₂ release falls/stops [1]; no NAD regenerated [1]; dehydrogenation stops [1] [3] (c) needed for ATP synthesis [1]; respiration coupled to ATP synthesis [1] [2]

items.stem: Name the products formed at the end of the electron transport chain.
items.answer: Water (from oxygen, electrons and protons).
items.markingKey: Water (from oxygen, electrons and protons) [1]

items.stem: Explain how the folding of the inner mitochondrial membrane increases the rate of ATP production.
items.answer: Cristae give a large surface area for many electron transport chains and ATP synthase molecules, so more oxidative phosphorylation per mitochondrion.
items.markingKey: large surface area [1]; more ETC / ATP synthase [1] [2]

items.stem: Assume that each reduced NAD gives 2.5 ATP and each reduced FAD gives 1.5 ATP by oxidative phosphorylation. What is the total number of ATP molecules made from one glucose molecule as a result of glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle, including any ATP made by substrate-linked phosphorylation.
items.markingKey: reduced NAD = 10, reduced FAD = 2 [1]; 10 × 2.5 + 2 × 1.5 = 28 [1]; + 4 substrate-linked = 32 [1] [3]

items.stem: Lucas measured the pH in the matrix of actively respiring mitochondria as 7.7 and in the intermembrane space as 7. (a) Explain how this difference in pH is produced. (b) Explain how this pH difference is used to make ATP.
items.answer: (a) Energy from electrons passing along the ETC is used to pump protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space. (b) Protons diffuse down their gradient through ATP synthase into the matrix; this drives phosphorylation of ADP to ATP (chemiosmosis).
items.markingKey: (a) ETC / electron flow [1]; protons pumped into intermembrane space [1] [2] (b) diffusion through ATP synthase [1]; ADP + Pi → ATP [1] [2]

items.stem: Arjun investigates two respiratory poisons on a suspension of isolated mitochondria supplied with a substrate, ADP and Pi. Carbon monoxide binds to cytochrome oxidase in place of oxygen. Oligomycin blocks the proton channel of ATP synthase. (a) Predict the effects of carbon monoxide on oxygen uptake and ATP synthesis. (b) Explain why electron transport and ATP synthesis are described as coupled. (c) Describe the role of the intermembrane space in chemiosmosis.
items.answer: (a) Electron flow to oxygen is blocked; oxygen uptake and ATP synthesis fall. (b) Electron transport pumps protons; the proton gradient is used to make ATP; if ATP synthesis stops, the gradient builds up and slows electron transport. (c) Protons are pumped into this small space so their concentration rises quickly, creating a steep gradient across the inner membrane.
items.markingKey: (a) electron flow to oxygen is blocked; oxygen uptake and ATP synthesis fall [2] (b) gradient links the two [1]; one cannot normally occur without the other [1] [2] (c) protons accumulate there [1]; small volume gives steep gradient [1] [2]

items.stem: Yeast in a sealed flask gives an RQ that rises from 1.0 to 3.5 over several hours. What is the best explanation?
options: The yeast has switched to respiring lipid
Oxygen is running out so more anaerobic respiration takes place
The yeast has begun to photosynthesise
items.answer: Oxygen is running out so more anaerobic respiration takes place
items.markingKey: CO₂ produced without O₂ uptake.

items.stem: Explain what happens to lactate after vigorous exercise in a mammal.
items.answer: Lactate is carried in the blood to the liver; it is oxidised back to pyruvate, which can be respired aerobically or converted to glucose/glycogen; the extra oxygen needed is the oxygen debt.
items.markingKey: transported to liver [1]; converted to pyruvate [1]; respired or to glucose/glycogen [1]; uses extra O₂ (debt) [1] [4]

items.stem: The equation for the complete aerobic respiration of palmitic acid is C₁₆H₃₂O₂ + 23O₂ → 16CO₂ + 16H₂O. Calculate the respiratory quotient (RQ).
Methylene blue decolourises more slowly when yeast is kept at 5 °C than at 30 °C. Why?
options: More oxygen dissolves at 5 °C and reduces the dye
Dehydrogenase enzymes work more slowly at the lower temperature
items.answer: Dehydrogenase enzymes work more slowly at the lower temperature
items.markingKey: Less kinetic energy, fewer collisions.

items.stem: Mateo investigated the effect of glucose concentration on the respiration of yeast. 2 cm³ of methylene blue was added to 10 cm³ of yeast suspension in glucose solution at 30 °C, and the time taken for the blue colour to disappear was recorded. Results table. Glucose concentration / %: 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4. Time for methylene blue to decolourise / s, trial 1: 491, 372, 264, 188, 131; trial 2: 464, 371, 268, 181, 130; trial 3: 465, 358, 260, 182, 125. Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: Independent: glucose concentration; dependent: time for methylene blue to decolourise.

items.answer: (a) Independent: glucose concentration; dependent: time for methylene blue to decolourise. (b) Temperature; volume and concentration of yeast suspension. (c) 8.96 s⁻¹
